sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Inti** ​(*inti*) — ‌Sun, Empire, ‌Agriculture ​· The ​solar ​father of ​the Inca ​— ‌belongs to ​the ​Incan tradition, ‌where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Sun, ​Empire, Agriculture". ​The ​name means ​"Sun"[^1].

**Inti** ​is ‌the sun ​as ‌sovereign: father ​of the ‌Inca ​dynasty, patron ‌of ​Cuzco, and ‌the divine ​ancestor ​whose rays ‌fed the ‌terraces ‌that fed ​an ​empire. He ‌is the ​unseen ​emperor of ‌the ​Andean sky ​— never ‌shown ​as a ‌body, only ​as ​gold, light, ​and ​the crimson ‌fringe on ‌his ​son's forehead.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling ‌**Inti** and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/inti/). ​The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*inti* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sources.citation: Juan de Betanzos, Suma y Narración de los Incas (1557).
Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica (1572).
Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653), books 13–14.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this ​name; ​**Inti** is ​a ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​of ‌the reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. ​Etymologically ‌the name ​means ​"Sun"[^1].

​The ​canonical ​spelling **Inti** ‌matches ​the ‌conventional ​scholarly romanization. ‌The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form ‌*inti* contains ​the ​same ‌letters, ‌so ‌no lost ​diacritics ​or ‌encoding ​transition is ​claimed. ‌The ​editorial ​work ‌is to ​fix ‌one ​reviewed ​reference ​spelling, preserve ​capitalization ‌and ‌provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original ​evidence ‌visible. ‌The displayed ‌form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ​computed ​from ‌the ​displayed form ​itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- **i** ​→ ‌**I** ​— ‌Same
- **n** ​→ ‌**n** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**t** → ​**t** ​— ​Same
- ​**i** ‌→ **i** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/inti/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**inti** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Inti.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Inti" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Inti" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"inti" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Inti ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Inti ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Inti ‌place ​sun, empire, ​agriculture ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

Inti ‌appears ​in ‌incan tradition ​as ​sun, empire, ​agriculture. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Sun", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ​and ‌Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ​and ‌later tradition-keepers ‌preserved ‌Inti in ​ritual, ​text, ‌and iconography, ​ensuring ​the ‌name survived ​into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

‌The ​myths of ​Inti ​survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ‌and ​later retellings. ‌Each ​version reflects ​the ‌interests ‌of its ‌tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ‌philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Inti ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Inti ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Incan ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Inti, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​sun ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Most ​sun gods ‌are clocks ‌or lamps. ​Inti ​is something ​rarer: a ​sun ​who is ‌also a ​father, a ​title, ‌and a ​border. To ‌be ​his child ‌was to ​hold an ​office; ​to hold ​the office ​was ‌to be ​luminous by ‌definition; and ​the ‌whole astonishing ​apparatus of ‌Inca ​civilization — ‌the terraces, ​the storehouses, ​the ‌road that ‌runs along ‌the ​equator — ​can be ‌read as ​a ​household administered ‌by the ​sun's ​eldest son. ‌The theology ​solved the ‌oldest ​problem of ​government: legitimacy. ​If ​the emperor ‌is the ‌sun's son, ​rebellion ‌is not ​politics but ​eclipse, ‌a darkness ‌no subject ‌can afford. ‌Yet ​there is ‌tenderness in ​it ​too: the ​Inca greeted ‌his father ​each ​morning, feasted ​him at ‌each ​solstice, and ​carried his ​image into ‌battle ​as a ‌banner of ​gold. ‌The name ​restored here ‌is the ‌shortest ​genealogy in ​the Americas: ​Inti ​— the ‌sun who ‌adopted a ​nation.[^1]
